prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

NEW DELHI, India (CNN) -- Hundreds of Indian army troops were using helicopters and boats Wednesday to deliver supplies and rescue villagers stranded by the worst flooding in decades, after the Kosi River breached an embankment in Nepal to the north. The death toll in the hard-to-reach Bihar state in northeastern India has been difficult to determine. Bihar emergency management official K.K. Agarwal confirmed 10 deaths to CNN on Wednesday, but the news agency Press Trust of India (PTI) reported 55. Phone lines and electricity are out in the flooded areas. In the Supaul district city of Birpur, Mohd Rauffudin's hopes were fading. He told IBN -- a CNN partner station in India -- that while he was trying to stay afloat, he lost contact with his wife and children, as well as his nine brothers and his parents. "I wish the help had reached (us) on time. That way at least my children could have been safe," he said. A woman who called herself Ruby told IBN her baby has been sick for four days, she can't reach medical help and she has lost track of her family. "My child is so ill. I cannot do a thing about it. I wonder what I did wrong that my child must suffer," the mother said. The flooding began when the river burst through an embankment in Nepal more than a week ago, swallowing villages and destroying about 225,000 homes, officials and UNICEF India said. Water flowed so forcefully from the breach that the river changed course, making a new channel about 75 miles (120km) east of its river bed, flooding areas unaccustomed to water that high.  Watch survivors find safety on roofs » . Agarwal said the disaster affected about 2 million people and 725 villages in Bihar, India's poorest state. Ninety-five relief shelters had been set up, 44 health-care camps and 22 shelters for animals, he said. Army spokesman Lt. Col. A. K. Mathur said 400 troops were involved in rescue operations, and the military had dispatched at least 20 rescue boats. Three army helicopters were dropping thousands of food packets, he said. PTI reported earlier in the day that bad weather had prevented Indian air force choppers from conducting relief drops in the worst-hit districts of Bihar: Supaul, Saharsa, Araria and Madhepura. Officials told CNN it was the worst flooding in Bihar in 80 years.  Watch more on people stranded » . The Kosi is known to Indians as the "River of Sorrow" because of its flooding during the monsoon season, which lasts from June to September. The river flows into the Hindu-revered Ganges River. Video has shown residents huddled atop low-rise buildings, standing in waist-high water in the streets and trying to escape in boats. The flooding has submerged roads and railway tracks, and cut off electricity.

NEW DELHI, India (CNN) — Indian military personnel used boats and helicopters on Wednesday to rescue trapped residents and distribute aid after the Kosi River broke through a levee in Nepal, causing Bihar’s most severe flooding in decades.

Because many affected communities in the northeastern Indian state are inaccessible, authorities have struggled to establish an accurate death toll. K.K. Agarwal, a Bihar emergency-management official, told CNN on Wednesday that 10 people had died, while the Press Trust of India (PTI) put the number at 55. Electricity and telephone service have been disrupted throughout the inundated region.

In Birpur, a city in Supaul district, Mohd Rauffudin said he was losing hope. He told IBN, CNN’s partner broadcaster in India, that as he fought to remain above water, he became separated from his wife and children, his parents and all nine of his brothers. He said that if assistance had arrived sooner, at least his children might have been saved.

Another survivor, who identified herself as Ruby, told IBN that her baby had been ill for four days. She said she had no access to medical care and did not know where her relatives were. Distraught, she said she was powerless to help her seriously sick child and wondered what she had done to deserve the child’s suffering.

The disaster began more than a week earlier when the Kosi burst through an embankment in Nepal. According to officials and UNICEF India, the resulting waters engulfed villages and ruined approximately 225,000 houses.

The flow through the breach was so powerful that the river shifted into a newly formed channel roughly 75 miles (120 kilometers) east of its previous bed. This sent unusually deep water into places that were not accustomed to such flooding, forcing some survivors to seek refuge on rooftops.

Agarwal said around 2 million people in 725 villages had been affected across Bihar, India’s poorest state. Authorities had established 95 relief centers, 44 medical camps and 22 facilities to shelter animals.

Army spokesman Lt. Col. A.K. Mathur said 400 soldiers were taking part in the rescue effort and that the military had deployed at least 20 boats. He added that three army helicopters were air-dropping thousands of food packages.

Earlier Wednesday, PTI reported that poor weather had stopped Indian air force helicopters from delivering supplies to Bihar’s four most severely affected districts: Supaul, Saharsa, Araria and Madhepura.

Officials told CNN that Bihar had not experienced flooding of this magnitude in 80 years.

In India, the Kosi is commonly called the “River of Sorrow” because it routinely floods during the monsoon period, which runs from June through September. It eventually joins the Ganges, a river considered sacred by Hindus.

Video footage showed people crowded onto the roofs of short buildings, wading through streets in waist-deep water and attempting to flee by boat. Roads and railroad lines were underwater, and power supplies had been severed.
outputs.L3:
Hundreds of Indian Army troops were deployed to rescue stranded villagers and deliver emergency supplies after the Kosi River breached an embankment in neighboring Nepal. Using helicopters and boats, rescue teams worked across the severely flooded areas of Bihar, where approximately 2 million people in 725 villages were affected. The disaster destroyed an estimated 225,000 homes, forcing large numbers of residents to seek shelter.

The death toll remained unclear. Government officials confirmed 10 fatalities, while the Press Trust of India reported that as many as 55 people had died.

The embankment breach caused the Kosi River to change course dramatically, carving out a new channel about 75 miles east of its original riverbed. As a result, water surged into communities that were not accustomed to severe flooding and were poorly prepared for such a disaster.

Authorities mobilized around 400 troops, at least 20 rescue boats, and three helicopters to support evacuation and relief operations. They also established temporary shelters, health-care camps, and facilities for displaced animals while continuing to distribute food and other essential supplies.
outputs.L4:
Indian troops deployed helicopters and boats to rescue stranded villagers and deliver food, drinking water, and other essential supplies after the Kosi River burst through an embankment in neighboring Nepal. The breach forced the river into an old channel, sending a vast surge of water across northern Bihar and producing the state’s worst flooding in decades.

Entire communities were inundated as the floodwaters spread across low-lying districts. Many residents took refuge on rooftops, embankments, roads, and other patches of high ground while waiting to be evacuated. Rescue teams struggled to reach isolated villages because roads and bridges had been submerged or damaged, leaving boats and aircraft as the only practical means of assistance in some areas.

At least 10 people were confirmed dead, although some estimates placed the toll as high as 55. Approximately 225,000 homes were destroyed, and around 2 million people in 725 villages were affected. Large numbers of livestock were also lost, while crops and farmland were left underwater, threatening the livelihoods of families dependent on agriculture.

Authorities established relief camps for displaced residents and distributed emergency supplies. However, the scale of the disaster created urgent shortages of shelter, clean water, food, medicine, and sanitation. Officials and aid workers also feared outbreaks of waterborne disease as contaminated floodwater surrounded crowded settlements and temporary camps.

The flooding was especially devastating because Bihar is India’s poorest state and many affected families had few resources with which to rebuild. The Kosi, often called the “Sorrow of Bihar” because of its history of destructive floods and shifting channels, once again demonstrated the region’s vulnerability. Beyond the immediate rescue effort, the disaster raised serious questions about embankment maintenance, cross-border water management, and the long-term protection of millions of people living along the river.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news report about the catastrophic Kosi River flooding in Bihar, India, including casualty estimates, rescue operations, survivor accounts, and the scale of the damage.
counterfactuals.output:
**Kosi River disaster leaves millions displaced in Bihar**

**PATNA, India —** Catastrophic flooding along the Kosi River has devastated large parts of Bihar after the river burst through an embankment in neighboring Nepal on August 18, 2008, abruptly changing course and sweeping across densely populated districts.

Indian authorities ultimately reported more than 400 deaths across Bihar, although the full toll remained difficult to determine as floodwaters isolated hundreds of villages. An estimated 3.3 million people were affected, and roughly one million were evacuated in what officials described as one of India’s largest civilian rescue operations.

The hardest-hit districts included Supaul, Madhepura, Araria, Saharsa and Purnia. Entire communities disappeared beneath muddy water as the Kosi flowed through a channel it had largely abandoned generations earlier. Hundreds of thousands of homes were damaged or destroyed, while vast areas of farmland, roads and public infrastructure were inundated.

The Indian military, air force, National Disaster Response Force and local agencies deployed boats and helicopters to reach stranded residents. Rescue crews ferried families from rooftops, trees and shrinking patches of high ground. Aircraft dropped food packets and drinking water into areas cut off by the flood.

Survivors arriving at relief camps described fleeing with little warning, carrying children and abandoning livestock, crops and possessions. Many said they had spent days without adequate food or clean water while waiting for boats. Families were separated during the evacuation, and overcrowded shelters struggled with shortages of sanitation, medicine and supplies.

Officials estimated that about 300,000 homes were destroyed and hundreds of thousands of hectares of crops were damaged. The loss of cattle, grain stocks and agricultural land threatened livelihoods long after the water receded.

The disaster was caused by a breach in the Kosi’s eastern embankment near Kusaha, Nepal. The failure diverted the river into older channels, sending a wall of water across areas that were not prepared for a major river flow.

Known as the “Sorrow of Bihar” because of its history of destructive floods and shifting channels, the Kosi left behind a humanitarian crisis stretching far beyond the initial emergency. Authorities warned that rebuilding homes, restoring farmland and preventing disease would take months, while questions mounted over embankment maintenance and whether the scale of the disaster could have been reduced.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Report on the worst flooding in Bihar in 80 years after the Kosi River breached an embankment in Nepal. Use a dateline, quotes from affected residents, and official relief statistics.
counterfactuals.output:
**KUSHAHA, Nepal/BHAGALPUR, India, Sept. 6, 2008** — The Kosi River has unleashed Bihar’s worst flooding in roughly 80 years after bursting through an embankment in southeastern Nepal and abandoning its established channel, sweeping across villages that had long been considered safe.

The breach occurred on Aug. 18 near Kushaha in Nepal’s Sunsari district. Instead of remaining within its embanked course, the Kosi surged into an older channel farther east, inundating large areas of Supaul, Madhepura, Araria, Saharsa and Purnia districts.

“The water came so quickly that we could not save anything,” one displaced farmer from Madhepura told relief workers after reaching a government camp. “We left with only the clothes we were wearing.”

Another resident, separated from members of her family during the evacuation, said: “Our house, grain and cattle are gone. We do not know where we will live when the water goes down.”

The flood stranded hundreds of thousands of people on rooftops, roads and patches of high ground. Boats operated by the Indian Army, Navy, National Disaster Response Force and local volunteers moved through submerged settlements, while helicopters dropped food packets and drinking water.

Official assessments later put the number of people affected at about **3.3 million across more than 1,000 villages**. Approximately **one million people were evacuated**, and more than **300,000 homes were damaged or destroyed**. Bihar authorities recorded **hundreds of deaths—about 500 in final official counts—**while acknowledging that the exact toll was difficult to establish because many people remained missing.

The state opened hundreds of relief camps and community kitchens, sheltering several hundred thousand evacuees at the height of the emergency. Authorities distributed rice, flattened rice, lentils, plastic sheeting, medicines and water-purification supplies. New Delhi declared the disaster a **“national calamity”** and announced central assistance, including food grain and emergency funding.

Relief operations were hampered by washed-out roads, strong currents and the enormous area under water. Health officials warned of diarrhoea, malaria and other diseases in crowded camps where clean water and sanitation were limited.

The Kosi, which descends from the Himalayas through Nepal, carries vast quantities of silt and has repeatedly changed course across the plains of northern Bihar. Known as the “Sorrow of Bihar,” it had been confined by embankments for decades before the Kushaha failure sent it back into a channel it had abandoned generations earlier.

For survivors, the scale of the loss remained difficult to absorb. “There is water everywhere,” an evacuee from Supaul said. “Our village has disappeared.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a detailed breaking-news article describing how Indian troops are using helicopters and boats to rescue villagers stranded by floods in northeastern India.
counterfactuals.output:
## BREAKING: Indian Troops Deploy Helicopters and Boats to Rescue Flood-Stranded Villagers in Northeast

*The following is a fictionalized breaking-news report based on a developing flood-rescue scenario.*

**GUWAHATI, India —** Indian military personnel used helicopters, inflatable boats and high-clearance vehicles on Tuesday to evacuate villagers stranded by severe flooding across northeastern India, as swollen rivers submerged roads, damaged bridges and cut off remote communities.

Rescue teams were operating in several low-lying districts after days of intense rainfall caused rivers and tributaries to overflow. In some villages, residents climbed onto rooftops or moved to schools, embankments and other elevated areas while waiting for assistance.

Military helicopters flew over inundated farmland and isolated settlements, lowering rescue personnel into locations that could not be reached by road. Aircrews evacuated children, older residents, pregnant women and people requiring medical care, while also dropping food, drinking water and emergency supplies.

On the ground, troops and disaster-response teams navigated strong currents in motorized and inflatable boats. Rescuers moved between partially submerged homes, sometimes using ropes to guide boats around debris, utility poles and damaged structures.

Television footage and images shared by emergency agencies showed soldiers carrying children through waist-deep water and helping residents board rescue craft with small bags of belongings. Livestock could be seen crowded onto patches of higher ground as families left flooded homes.

Authorities warned that rescue operations were being complicated by continuing rain, poor visibility and the loss of road access. Landslides were also reported in hilly areas, raising concerns that additional communities could become isolated.

Temporary relief camps were being established in schools and government buildings outside the worst-affected zones. Officials said evacuees were being provided with cooked meals, bottled or purified water, blankets, basic medicines and sanitation supplies.

Medical teams were monitoring displaced residents for injuries and waterborne illnesses. Floodwater can contaminate wells and local water systems, increasing the risk of diarrhea, skin infections and other diseases, particularly among children.

State emergency officials said they were coordinating with the Indian Army, Air Force, local police and national disaster-response personnel. Additional boats, communications equipment and medical supplies were being moved toward affected areas.

The northeastern region experiences seasonal flooding during the monsoon, particularly in the Brahmaputra river basin. The scale and speed of inundation can leave rural communities with little time to evacuate, especially when rainfall upstream causes rivers to rise rapidly.

Authorities urged residents in vulnerable areas to follow evacuation instructions, avoid crossing flooded roads and move to designated shelters. More rainfall was possible, and rescue teams were expected to continue operations through the night where conditions allowed.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft an international news story about the humanitarian crisis caused by monsoon flooding along India’s “River of Sorrow,” with information from CNN, PTI, UNICEF, military officials, and survivors.
counterfactuals.output:
**Flooding along India’s ‘River of Sorrow’ triggers humanitarian crisis**

**PATNA, India —** Monsoon flooding along the Kosi River, widely known as Bihar’s “River of Sorrow,” has inundated communities across the eastern Indian state, forcing mass evacuations and leaving families in urgent need of food, clean water, shelter and medical care.

The flooding began after the Kosi overwhelmed or breached flood defenses, allowing water to spread across densely populated rural districts. CNN and India’s Press Trust of India reported widespread damage to villages, roads and farmland, with many residents stranded on rooftops, embankments and other patches of high ground.

Indian military officials said soldiers, air force helicopters and disaster-response teams had been deployed to rescue marooned residents and deliver emergency supplies. Rescue operations have been complicated by strong currents, submerged roads and the scale of the affected area.

Survivors described escaping with little more than the clothes they were wearing. Some said rising water arrived so quickly that they had no time to save livestock, food stocks or important documents. Families reaching relief camps faced overcrowding and uncertainty over when they might be able to return home.

UNICEF warned that children were among those most at risk. Floodwater can contaminate drinking supplies and increase the threat of diarrhea, cholera and other waterborne illnesses, while crowded shelters raise concerns about sanitation, nutrition and the protection of children separated from their families.

Aid workers were distributing drinking water, food, medicines and sanitation materials, but access remained difficult in isolated areas. Pregnant women, infants, older people and those with chronic illnesses were considered especially vulnerable.

The Kosi, which flows from Nepal into Bihar before joining the Ganges, has repeatedly changed course and caused destructive floods across the region. Its history of breaching embankments and sweeping through settlements earned it the “River of Sorrow” nickname.

Authorities said the full human and economic toll would not be clear until waters receded. With further monsoon rain possible, military teams and humanitarian agencies were racing to reach communities still cut off by the flooding.

*Source note: This draft synthesizes reporting and information attributed to CNN, PTI, UNICEF, Indian military officials and flood survivors. Current casualty, displacement and relief figures should be verified against the latest dated reports before publication.*
